summary: How radar finds range from an echo, matches pulses to the range, and what its parts, antennas and safety rules do.

blocks.title: How radar works
items: Echoes: radar sends a short pulse, then listens. The delay gives range; the antenna's direction gives bearing.
Band: SHF, super high frequency, 3 to 30 GHz. Most ship radars use X-band, near 9.4 GHz.
Pulse width (PW): 0.05 to 1.0 µs. Pulse repetition rate (PRR): 500 to 2,000 pulses per second (pps), the pulse rate of the magnetron.
Long ranges: a wide pulse carries more energy; a slow rate lets far echoes return.
Short ranges: a narrow pulse gives fine detail and a short minimum range; a fast rate gives more hits per sweep.

items.means: η: efficiency. d: dish diameter. λ: wavelength. Double the frequency: λ halves, gain × 4, up 6 dB. Beamwidth is about 70λ/d degrees.

blocks.title: Waveguides and antennas
items: Conductance: through electromagnetic and electrostatic fields in the walls of the waveguide.
Coupling energy in and out: a thin piece of wire as an antenna. A J-hook extracts the signal.
Slotted array: the common ship antenna. As gain increases, beamwidth decreases.

blocks.title: Safety and equipment
items: Before testing: first assure no personnel are in front of the antenna.
Magnetron magnet: keep metal tools away, no excessive heat, no shocks or blows.

blocks.title: Exam traps
items: PRR isn't the duty cycle's reciprocal.
TR (transmit-receive) guards the receiver; ATR (anti-transmit-receive) keeps the received signal out of the transmitter.
Thyratron, SCR and klystron don't make the output power.
Keeping the TR tuned is NOT a magnetron precaution.
Dish gain: 6 dB, not 3. Don't forget the square.
Collision avoidance uses gyrocompass, position receiver and speed indicator, not the anemometer.
